resources.string: Copy each game as a folder (with eboot.bin and sce_sys/) into\n%1$s\nor add another folder where you already keep them.

Vulkan renders and presents directly (fastest). OpenGL ES shows the final frame through EGL, a compatibility path for devices with a broken Vulkan present path; falls back to Vulkan when unsupported. Applies from the next game start.

Mali only, with the Vulkan backend: run on a Vulkan 1.3 instance (the default) or a Vulkan 1.1 one. 1.1 helps Mali drivers whose 1.3 path misbehaves or that expose the required features only through extensions. Applies from the next game start.
Per axis: a 4K game at 50 % renders at 1080p (a quarter of the work). Lower resolution relieves the GPU; some games do not support it
Unreal Engine games render near 4K and are slow on mobile GPUs; used unless the game has its own setting
Avoids stutter; an object may take a moment to appear
Ring for CPU-updated data. Some games fill 64 MB every frame and wait on the GPU; a larger ring avoids that, but may cause visual glitches in a few titles
KB downloaded in one wait when a game reads GPU-written buffers page by page (one launch title\'s render thread). Larger can speed up sequential reads; too large wastes bandwidth on random access
Unreal titles poll completion with millions of spin-yields; after a burst a short sleep releases the core and the power budget. Off restores pure sched_yield (may help or hurt per title)
Detailed hot-path logging to logcat, for bug reports; slows the game while enabled
Submit to the GPU after every release event. Slower (a blocking submit per fence), but use if a game waits forever on a fence (stuck graphics after loading screens)
Imported Turnip (Adreno) or PanVK (Mali); System uses the vendor driver
Community Turnip (Adreno) or PanVK (Mali) builds; the one you install becomes the global driver

FPS, CPU, GPU, RAM and temperatures on screen
Keep the emulation and graphics threads on the fastest CPU cores (big.LITTLE).

Low latency keeps triple buffering (default); VSync paces to the display for the smoothest image; Uncapped presents every finished frame for the highest frame rate (may tear). Applies from the next game start.

Bandwidth-tuned defaults for Mali GPUs (same graphics): hardware render-target clears that keep AFBC compression alive, a 128 MB streaming buffer and one more pipeline worker. Auto applies it only on Mali GPUs; applies from the next game start.

Snapdragon-tuned defaults (same graphics): a 128 MB streaming buffer, one more shader-compile worker and an extra swapchain image for high-refresh presenting. Auto applies it only on Adreno GPUs; applies from the next game start.

Display mode and emulated vblank for games paced by vblank (same graphics): Auto follows the display’s highest rate, so 90/120 Hz screens stop capping games at 60 FPS; 60 keeps the previous behaviour. Applies from the next game start.

Fills idle display ticks with a generated in-between frame, so the presented image runs at the display rate. Real frames are untouched and still appear the moment they finish, so input response stays the same. On by default where the GPU has headroom (off on Mali and older Adreno chips); turn it on or off at will. Applies from the next game start.
Clear this game\'s overrides (options and GPU driver).
Lower the render scale while the game cannot hold its frame rate and raise it back when there is headroom. Applies without restarting.
In automatic mode they hide when a physical controller is connected
Automatic: with the touch controls · Always: also with a physical controller
Nintendo swaps A↔B and X↔Y in games (controllers like the Odin\'s)
Move and resize the on-screen buttons to fit your hands
Drag a cluster to move it, tap to select

In the logs folder of your main folder

string-array.name: whats_new_items
string-array.item: New: frame generation (Settings → Performance, on by default). Idle display ticks now show a generated in-between frame instead of a repeat, so the presented image follows the display\'s rate — real frames still appear the moment they finish and input response is unchanged. Turn it off if you prefer the raw cadence.

Faster: the engine now recognises each game\'s workload on the fly (high-throughput 3D, layered compositing, forward-rendered 3D) and tunes its submit batching, download read-ahead and shader-compile workers to match, with a Mali/Adreno ladder per tier and a 4K policy of its own. The perf overlay shows the active engine family (T500/T501/T502).

New: a Vulkan version option on Mali (Settings → Graphics; 1.3 default, 1.1 for drivers that prefer it) and a custom on-screen controls editor (Settings → Controls) — move, resize and save your own button layout.

Fixed: the freezes. A game could freeze for whole seconds and come back — and the worst sessions died on a crash right after the freeze. The freeze came from the shader pipeline: when a draw needed a pipeline that was still compiling, the renderer waited for the compile with no limit at all, so a storm of new shaders (a new area, material streaming) could park the whole renderer behind the compile queue for tens of seconds. No draw may wait more than 4 milliseconds now (debug.capy.pipeline_wait_ms): past the bound the draw is skipped, the compile lands in the background, and the next time the game draws it renders for real — the 28-second class of freezes is gone by construction. The same serialization was the 1–3 FPS crawl in heavy 3D games: frames flow again while the pipelines warm up.

Fixed: the crash right after a freeze. The game’s own render worker, starved by the freeze above, timed out and tore its objects down, then wrote through the nulled pointer to address 0x1 — the session died with “the game made a null-pointer write”. Every such write below 64 KiB (the null guard page: it can never hold game data and nothing can ever read it back) is now skipped and the session continues, exactly like the read side already answers it with zeroes. A genuine null-write loop still gets the honest crash report (debug.capy.wild_store_recovery).

Fixed: the library could crash the app on a duplicate entry (“Key … was already used”). The list is now deduplicated inside the game grid itself, so no future source of the list can crash the interface, whatever produced it.

New: a Graphics API option (Settings → Graphics, also per game). Vulkan stays the default — it renders and presents directly. The new OpenGL ES mode is a compatibility path for devices whose Vulkan present path is broken: the final frame goes to an AHardwareBuffer that EGL/OpenGL ES shows on the same screen, same pixels, and the core falls back to Vulkan automatically whenever the device cannot do it (debug.capy.gl_backend).

Faster: every translated shader now runs through a per-vendor spirv-opt pass list before it reaches the GPU driver — the full list on Mali, a lighter one on Adreno. Dead branches and dead code, redundant loads and constants, dead vector lanes and duplicated types disappear, and the module comes out smaller and simpler: pipeline compiles finish sooner (fewer first-visit hitches and shorter shader-storm warm-ups) and mobile compilers generate better code. The optimized module is validated before use; on any failure the original is kept (debug.capy.spirv_opt).

Faster: emulated mesh draws — the heaviest 3D scenes — no longer stall the whole pipeline around every dispatch. Their barrier now covers exactly the vertex and compute accesses the mesh buffer needs, so other draws’ fragment work keeps flowing on Snapdragon and Mali.

Fixed: the crash from the latest report — a Unity-engine title could die the moment you switched apps or opened the volume menu. Its render worker read through a torn pointer into a never-mapped hole of the guest address space right after the window lost focus; that read now returns zero (the hole cannot hold game data) and the session keeps running (debug.capy.wild_read_recovery).

Fixed: the Mali performance regression and heavy frame drops. The Q2 refresh unlock ran the emulated vblank at the display’s maximum — 120 Hz on most phones — so the present thread woke twice as often, held the very locks the game threads need and woke guest vblank waiters twice per frame, all while the game could not even fill 60 FPS. The vblank is now governed: it paces at 60 Hz and unlocks to the display rate only while the game sustains 55+ FPS (two full one-second windows), so high refresh is kept by games that earn it and stops taxing games that cannot (debug.capy.vblank_governor).

Faster: the vblank tick itself got a fast path — event queues are no longer copied and no wake-up syscall is made for ports nobody listens on (that happened 60–120 times per second per open port before), and the present thread now runs on the big cores with the emulator and GPU threads (debug.capy.vblank_fastpath).

Fixed: frame drops from memory stalls. Guest memory is backed by 4 KiB pages on Android again — under the pressure a heavy game creates, a 2 MiB huge-page allocation could stall for milliseconds inside the kernel’s memory compaction, the signature of the “many drops” reports. Desktop builds keep huge pages (debug.capy.thp re-enables them). Mali also returns to the 256 KB download read-ahead window — it is bandwidth-bound; Adreno keeps the wider one.

Smoother on Snapdragon too: the same governor removes the 90/120 Hz pacing overhead from games that cannot fill it, and the vblank fast path cuts the per-tick cost on every GPU. Closing a video port now also wakes its waiters instead of risking a sleep-forever.

Fixed: heavy Unreal Engine titles no longer crash seconds into gameplay. GPU-driven draw batches read their draw counts and arguments from game memory that the game can free; a read that landed on freed memory killed the app (a host fault inside the draw code). Those reads are now guarded - a batch whose arguments vanished is skipped, exactly like a real GPU reading zero - and the page is never trusted again from that thread. The session keeps running (debug.capy.guarded_reads).

New: the 60 FPS ceiling is gone. The emulated vblank was fixed at 60 Hz, which capped every game paced by vblank even on 90/120 Hz screens. A new per-game Refresh rate option (Settings → Performance, Auto by default) now runs the display at its highest mode, tells Android and the game surface to keep it, and drives the emulated vblank at the same rate - same graphics, up to twice the frame rate on high-refresh screens.

New: Adreno GPU optimization (Settings → Performance, Auto on Snapdragon): a 128 MB streaming buffer, one more shader-compile worker (Turnip compiles slower than the stock driver) and an extra swapchain image so high-refresh presenting never throttles.

New: hot-pipeline compilation. During material streaming the shader queue could hold hundreds of one-shot pipelines while the game waited on the handful it was actively drawing with - draws were skipped and heavy games crawled. Pipelines the game re-requests now jump the queue and compile first (debug.capy.hot_pipelines), on every GPU.

Faster: queue submissions batch up to 16 deep on Mali/Adreno (was 8 - every vkQueueSubmit has fixed driver overhead that dominates at low FPS), the per-thread guest read cache grows from 2 MB to 16 MB of coverage under the GPU profiles (far fewer page-probe syscalls in Unreal titles), and GPU download read-ahead widens to 512 KB (debug.capy.read_ahead_kb).

Fixed: the app could crash right after an import — the same file could enter the library twice, which the game grid cannot show, and a second pick while a copy was still running raced the first one. Both are impossible now, and picking a real .pkg says what to import instead of a generic rejection. A one-off null-pointer read inside the game no longer ends the session either: the read returns zero and the game keeps running (limited, reads only — debug.capy.null_read_recovery).
Faster: big imports copy with a 1 MB buffer and the progress redraws once per percent instead of once per chunk, so the interface stays responsive while gigabytes are written.

Fixed: importing a large game (a 7 GB eboot) no longer eats 17+ GB of storage and fails with “not enough space”. Imports now land in the library folder instead of internal storage, a failed import deletes its partial file (older versions left a multi-GB leftover behind on every retry — leftovers are cleaned automatically on start), and free space is re-checked while copying.

New: much deeper Mali optimization, same graphics. Render targets now keep Arm\'s AFBC lossless compression alive (a single-format view list instead of an open-ended mutable format list, which had forced the driver to disable compression) — far less memory traffic per frame. Games that reinterpret target memory get a one-time copy and stay correct. Also benefits Adreno (UBWC).

New: async-compute submissions are batched like graphics ones while more work is queued (fewer vkQueueSubmit per frame), and the output stage takes a 1:1 copy instead of a scaled blit when the frame matches the screen exactly.

New: Mali GPU optimization (Settings → Performance, Auto by default). On Mali GPUs (Mali-G76 class and newer) the emulator switches to hardware render-target clears that keep Arm\'s AFBC compression alive, a 128 MB streaming buffer, one more pipeline-compile worker and render passes that are no longer split by game events — the same graphics with far less memory traffic.

New: deep performance pass for every GPU — same graphics, same pixels. Game partial-flush and writeback events no longer split the open render pass (their barrier now fires at the pass end), removing hundreds of full render-target store+reload cycles per frame on tile-based GPUs (Mali, Adreno). Cache reclamation runs at a fixed cadence instead of after every submission, shader warm-up gets more compile workers on 8+-core devices, and the streaming ring grows to 96 MB on non-Mali GPUs.
New: the per-game options panel ("Choose options for this game") now scrolls, so save export / import, reset and Play are always reachable on small screens (and gamepad focus follows the rows).
